title: Sovereign Escape Velocity: Ownership w Open Models — Gus Martins, & Ian Ballantyne, Google DeepMind
talk_summary: A Google DeepMind Gemma product talk arguing that open-weight models (Gemma 4: 26B MoE with 4B active params, 31B dense, E2B/E4B edge) let you own/self-host models for cost control, privacy, and sovereignty, with concrete guidance to drop them into existing OpenAI-compatible workflows and build your own evals. Most of the content is model marketing and mobile demos; the transferable parts are the cost-threshold framing for offloading high-token agentic work to cheap/self-hosted models and the 'evaluate on your own tasks' discipline.

takeaways.technique: Task-threshold routing to cheap/self-hosted models for high-token agentic work
takeaways.what_they_do: Frame model choice as thresholds: does the model fit the hardware, meet the latency need, and beat cloud cost — then offload suitable high-token tasks (refactoring, small modular code gen, doc processing) to small open models while keeping frontier models for hard architecture work.
takeaways.evidence_quote: what it is very good at doing is following very specific instructions about doing things like refactoring analyzing uh generating code in uh in small modular bits
takeaways.numbers: 31B runs on one GPU vs competitors needing ~200GB / 4-5 GPUs; 26B MoE ~26GB RAM with context on a 48GB M4 Mac

takeaways.technique: Own the inference for sunken-cost hardware
takeaways.what_they_do: Argue that once you own GPUs, marginal token cost becomes energy/utilization rather than per-token API price, so high-token agentic workloads (programming is among the highest token consumers) benefit most from self-hosting.
takeaways.evidence_quote: whereas we're not paying for uh the price of these agents or models within tokens, we're actually paying for them in terms of energy costs
takeaways.numbers: programming cited as among highest input+output token tasks on OpenRouter

takeaways.technique: Per-task eval suites over generic benchmarks
takeaways.what_they_do: Recommend dropping a candidate model into existing workflows to see what it handles, then bolstering your own evaluation suites because benchmark scores don't predict performance on your specific tasks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: how good the model is depends on how well it does on your task and not anybody else's task

takeaways.technique: OpenAI-compatible endpoint swap for cheap experimentation
takeaways.what_they_do: Show that trying a new model is a one-line change if you point any OpenAI-compatible client at a local server (Ollama/LM Studio) and pick the model name.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can take any open AI compatible interface that you've got and you can point it at a service like Olama or LM LM LM Studio

takeaways.technique: Match model size to hardware tier (edge/single-GPU) for batch vs interactive work
takeaways.what_they_do: Distinguish latency-sensitive interactive tasks from offline/batch tasks, and pick model size and execution timing accordingly (e.g. background processing at night).
takeaways.evidence_quote: is it something that you can process offline as a background task when they plug their phone in at night
